extracted.intended_audience: federal agency economists and regulatory analysts preparing benefit-cost and regulatory impact analyses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting and applying discounting methods and parameters (social rate of time preference, shadow price of capital, Ramsey and long-term approaches) in U.S. federal regulatory benefit-cost analysis under OMB Circular A-4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adjust the discount rate for uncertainty; use certainty equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: “the discount rate should not be adjusted to account for the uncertainty of future benefits and costs; instead, allowance for uncertainty should be made by adjusting the monetary values of changes in benefits or costs (for the year in which they occur) so that they are expressed in terms of their certainty equivalents.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use certainty-equivalent valuations to capture uncertainty in benefits/costs rather than adding a default risk premium to the discount rate. This is OMB’s general recommendation (as repeated from 1996).

rubrics_metrics.name: When certainty equivalents do not fully capture risk, treat risk as an unquantified bias
rubrics_metrics.description: “When certainty equivalents are not calculated in a way that fully captures risk (including both idiosyncratic and systematic risk), risk should be thought of like other regulatory effects for which agencies lack reliable measurements: that is, as a non-monetized benefit or cost.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot robustly compute certainty-equivalents, document risk qualitatively and recognize it as an unquantified source of bias rather than defaulting to an unjustified numerical risk premium on the discount rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the shadow price of capital (SPC) to account for regulatory effects on capital
rubrics_metrics.description: “The shadow price of capital (SPC) approach converts all benefits and costs into consumption-equivalent values before discounting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB considers the SPC approach analytically preferred for regulations that substantially affect capital incidence because it maps effects into consumption-equivalent terms appropriate for discounting at the social rate of time preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default SPC values: use two defaults 1.0 (open economy) and 1.2 (closed economy) for sensitivity testing
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB proposed that when evaluating regulations anticipated to have substantial incidence on capital, agencies should use—as a default—two shadow prices of capital. The first, 1.0, reflects an open economy estimate... The second recommended SPC, 1.2, reflects a closed economy estimate with no foreign capital flows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SPC = 1.0 and SPC = 1.2 as default boundary cases in regulatory analyses to test sensitivity to capital incidence. OMB views 1.2 as a well-supported, conservative outer-bound for sensitivity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct sensitivity analysis using two outer-bound incidence cases on capital
rubrics_metrics.description: “[A]nalyzing two outer-bound cases: one assuming all benefits and no costs fall on capital, and another assuming all costs and no benefits fall on capital.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run analyses under the two extreme incidence assumptions to identify when SPC or regulation-specific capital-incidence estimation would materially change conclusions and thereby warrant further, more detailed analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: If regulation likely has little or no incidence on capital, discount at the social rate of time preference (SRTP)
rubrics_metrics.description: “In certain cases, it may be clear that your regulation likely has little or no incidence on capital... In such cases, you can simply discount at the social rate of time preference.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SRTP when regulatory costs/benefits predominantly affect consumption (e.g., costs passed through to consumers) or when magnitudes on capital are negligible or constant across periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use pre-tax market return (e.g., 7%) as the social discount rate
rubrics_metrics.description: “the 7% rate used to estimate the opportunity cost of capital represents a pre-tax rate of return that is not risk-free. The social rate of time preference estimate in the revised guidance is meant to apply to a risk-free (or, e.g., certainty-equivalent) stream of regulatory benefits and costs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating historical pre-tax returns to capital (such as the 2003-era 7%) as the SRTP; those rates reflect market returns including risk premia and distortions and are not appropriate for discounting certainty-equivalent regulatory streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use defaults to identify when to do regulation-specific SPC estimation; do not require it in every case
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is not feasible or desirable for agencies to devote analytic resources to that determination in every case. OMB believes that the defaults it has put forward help to identify cases where further analysis... are likely to be most informative.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply default SPC values and sensitivity tests first; only invest resources in bespoke SPC or capital-incidence estimation when sensitivity analysis indicates results are materially sensitive to those assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB will not prescribe one precise parameterization for SPC; rely on range of high-quality literature
rubrics_metrics.description: “Because the estimate relies on a variety of different approaches, parameterizations, and modeling assumptions across economic literature... no specific set of parameters can be provided by OMB.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept use of values supported by multiple credible approaches in the literature; agencies need not adopt a single OMB-prescribed parameter set if the choice is defensible and documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adopt approaches that assume all costs fall on capital and no benefits do (e.g., Kolb & Scheraga 1990)
rubrics_metrics.description: One group of commenters proposed using the Kolb and Scheraga (1990) approach, which would—among other things—assume that all initial regulatory costs accrue to capital and no benefits accrue to capital. OMB is not adopting this approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that regulations can both induce and displace investment; analytical approaches should allow for benefits or costs to fall on capital or consumption and identify the relevant range of circumstances where SPC matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider evidence on capital mobility and market frictions when judging SPC lower-bound plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB argues that U.S. capital markets have generally become more open and that evidence (e.g., low Treasury premia relative to peers) supports considering an open-economy lower-bound SPC of 1.0, while acknowledging some domestic frictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate capital mobility, access to banking and global capital markets, and sector-specific borrowing frictions when deciding whether an open-economy SPC assumption (1.0) is reasonable for sensitivity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ramsey discounting may be used only with OMB consultation; default remains descriptive market-rate approach
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB is adopting its proposal to permit agencies to use a Ramsey discounting approach when appropriate, but only after conferring with OMB. OMB has decided to reduce Circular A-4’s discussion of the Ramsey approach at this time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Ramsey calibration involves contested parameter choices and links discount rates to growth, agencies should generally rely on observed market rates for near-term discounting and seek OMB concurrence before employing Ramsey-based or structural model-based discounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: For long-term discounting, account for ethical considerations and uncertainty by considering declining discount rates
rubrics_metrics.description: “Special ethical considerations arise when comparing benefits and costs across generations... A distinct reason for discounting the benefits and costs accruing to future generations at a lower rate is uncertainty about the appropriate value of the discount rate... the certainty-equivalent discount rate will have a declining schedule.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For very long horizons, consider declining discount rate schedules justified by uncertainty about long-term growth and intergenerational ethics; document normative choices if adopting prescriptive lower rates for distant futures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and disclose other potential unquantified biases affecting SRTP and discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Other factors—such as behavioral biases, zero lower bound periods, liquidity premia, term premia, default risk, and taxation of income on Federal debt instruments—bias the SRTP estimate (and thus the discount rate) upwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge these potential sources of upward bias when estimating or selecting SRTP and discuss them qualitatively or via sensitivity analysis if quantitative adjustment is infeasible.
